title: KV cache: NUMA-aware arenas + buddy allocator notes
content:
Purpose

This doc captures a focused implementation sketch and open questions for a KV cache memory layout that aims to reduce cross-NUMA latency, limit fragmentation, and support predictable eviction across multi-tenant workloads. It is intended as a working design for the serving runtime team — not final.

Context / why this came up

- Current KV cache experiments show 10–40% tail-latency variance on multi-socket machines when memory allocations cross NUMA boundaries.
- Fragmentation from mixed-size block churn (short-lived chat contexts vs long-lived embeddings) causes increased OOMs and more frequent expensive compaction passes.
- Existing slab-ish designs help for fixed-size entries but are inefficient when entry sizes vary and when tenants share capacity.

Design goals (prioritized)

1) NUMA locality: prefer allocations and eviction choices that are local to the requesting CPU socket.
2) Low fragmentation: avoid wasted internal/external fragmentation that increases memory pressure.
3) Predictable performance: minimize global pauses/compactions and bound allocation cost per request.
4) Multi-tenant fairness: eviction decisions should respect per-tenant quotas and prioritized fallbacks.
5) Graceful degradation: when memory is tight, degrade to simpler eviction strategies instead of heavy compaction.

High-level approach

- Partition physical memory into NUMA-aware arenas (one arena per NUMA node). Each arena manages its own pools and allocator structures (no cross-node allocations unless explicitly allowed by policy).
- Within an arena, use a hybrid allocator: buddy allocator for variable-size allocations plus a small set of fixed-size slab pools for very common small sizes (16B, 64B, 256B, 1KB).
- Maintain per-arena free-lists, LRU rings, and tenant accounting. Global coordination is asynchronous: a background rebalancer may move cold objects between arenas or trigger controlled fallbacks.

Memory layout and invariants

- Arena = contiguous region of physical RAM bound to a NUMA node. Implementation: mmap with flags for NUMA binding (or use libnuma APIs).
- Each arena exposes two allocation paths: fast-path (slab or single-bucket buddy) with lock-free or fine-grained locks for hot-path allocations; slow-path for large/rare allocations involving metadata updates.
- Keep metadata compact and cache-friendly: use 64-bit headers where possible; align frequently-read metadata to cacheline boundaries.
- Invariant: allocations from arena A should remain pinned to A unless explicitly migrated by the rebalancer or during eviction compaction.

Allocator details

1) Slab pools (hot small objects)
- Sizes: 16B, 64B, 256B, 1KB — chosen based on telemetry (we should validate with a sampling run).
- Each slab is itself allocated from the arena using the buddy allocator in slab-sized chunks (e.g., 2MB huge slab region per slab class to reduce header overhead).
- Free lists per-CPU for lock-free fast-path; fall back to a per-arena lock-protected list when cross-CPU necessary.
- Purpose: minimize internal fragmentation and fast allocation for hot ephemeral KV entries (chat prefixes, state).

2) Buddy allocator (variable sized)
- Use a power-of-two buddy allocator for variable allocation sizes > 1KB up to a configurable max (e.g., 2MB), with size classes at powers of two.
- A single buddy block maps to a run that the allocator splits/merges; merging is allowed only inside the same arena to avoid moving pages across NUMA.
- To reduce external fragmentation, the buddy allocator supports an eager coalescing policy during background idle windows and a conservative policy on allocation path to keep latency down.

3) Large object allocator
- Allocate directly from OS (mmap/hugepages) for very large objects (>= configurable threshold, e.g., 8MB). Mark them as pinned to a NUMA node.
- Maintain a small bitmap/radix map to look up object ownership and tenant mappings.

Fragmentation mitigation strategies

- Size-class migration: periodic aggregator samples objects by age + size. If a size class shows high fragmentation (lots of partially used buddy pages), trigger compaction inside the arena to repack live objects into fewer blocks and free whole buddy blocks.
- Per-tenant reservation & soft-limits: map tenants to soft-reservations — allow tenants to burst above reservation if capacity available, but eviction will respect reservations. This reduces churn from noisy neighbors.
- GC-ish reclaim sweep: lightweight sweep that identifies cold entries (LRU tail, low access rate) and reclaims them without heavy copying when possible. For non-copy reclaim, mark blocks stale and eventually free when the refcount hits zero.
- Prefer slab allocation for small frequent objects to prevent them from scattering across buddy blocks.

Eviction policy and multi-tenant considerations

- Eviction operates primarily at arena scope. Reasons: locality and to avoid cross-node memory traffic.
- Use a two-tier eviction heuristic: tenant-aware cost estimation + age/access frequency. Score = alpha * estimated_cost + beta * age_rank + gamma * tenant_penalty. Tune weights per workload.
- Implement a fast path LRU approximation (clock or segmented LRU) for per-arena hot caches to keep eviction O(1).
- For multi-tenant fairness, maintain tenant quotas and a backpressure signal to upper layers when eviction rates exceed thresholds. Also include a low-priority eviction queue for background compaction reclaimed items.

Migration and rebalancing

- Migration is expensive. Strategy: avoid eager cross-NUMA migration. Only migrate on either: (a) explicit admin policy, (b) arena imbalance exceeding threshold for a sustained period, (c) object pinning requests.
- Migration works in phases: copy-on-write + pointer swap + epoch sync to avoid exposing torn reads. Prefer migrating cold objects only.

Telemetry and metrics to collect (prototype plan)

- Per-arena allocation latency distribution (P50/P95/P99).
- Fraction of allocations served by local arena vs remote (cross-NUMA).
- Fragmentation metrics: per-arena free-buddy-block-count-by-order, total external/internal fragmentation ratio, slab utilization per-size-class.
- Eviction metrics: evictions/sec by tenant, eviction score distribution, mistaken-eviction ratio (evicted then immediately reaccessed).
- Compaction overhead: CPU and wall-time used for compaction per GB reclaimed.

Operational knobs (runtime config)

- arena_size: baseline bytes per NUMA arena (default: auto-detect physical numa-local mem / #arenas).
- slab_sizes: list of small slab sizes active.
- large_object_threshold: bytes.
- eager_coalesce_window: seconds of idle time before aggressive merging.
- tenant_soft_reservations: map tenant->bytes (admin settable).
- migration_enabled: bool (default false in first rollout).

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve

- Buddy vs custom segregated free lists: buddies are simpler but wasteful for highly heterogeneous sizes. Should we implement a best-fit small-block allocator instead for mid-size (1–64KB) ranges?
- How aggressively to coalesce during normal operation — cost of coalescing can add latency; background compaction is better but needs tuning.
- Should eviction ever pull remote arena memory (cross-NUMA) if local arena is full but global free exists? This reduces fragmentation but increases latency for subsequent accesses.
- Hardware hugepages: should slabs come from hugepages to reduce TLB pressure? Pros: fewer TLB misses for large working sets. Cons: fragmentation and harder to reclaim.
- How to handle pinning for workloads that explicitly need KV on specific GPUs/NUMA nodes? Pointer indirections + explicit pin metadata? More design needed.

Prototype plan and milestones (rough)

- Week 0–2: implement arena abstraction + per-arena metadata and mmap NUMA binding. Add basic per-arena buddy allocator and unit tests.
- Week 3–4: add small slab pools, per-CPU fast-path free lists. Run microbenchmarks with synthetic alloc patterns.
- Week 5–6: implement per-arena eviction ring + tenant accounting. Hook basic eviction policy.
- Week 7–8: add background compaction (eager coalesce window) and basic telemetry. Run end-to-end workload against local cluster.
- Week 9: incremental experiments: enable migration_enabled=true in a canary cluster and measure cross-NUMA traffic and tail latency.

Back-of-envelope performance expectations

- Fast-path allocations (slab) should be sub-microsecond on uncontended per-CPU path.
- Buddy allocations under moderate contention: low single-digit microseconds.
- Compaction cost depends on live fraction; expect 1–5s CPU per GB reclaimed in early prototype unless optimized copy paths / hugepages used.

Notes to self / action items

- Michael: add synthetic traces from production (short context vs long-lived embedding keys) so we can tune slab sizes.
- Priya: prototype telemetry counters in the allocator hooks (per-arena).
- Evan: spike a simple compaction run and measure copy bandwidth with and without hugepages.
- TODO: file follow-up RFC if prototype metrics show >25% reduction in fragmentation and tail-latency improvements.

References and inspiration

- Memcached slab allocator and tcmalloc concepts (segregated fits / per-thread caches).
- Buddy allocators in kernel memory management; NUMA-aware allocation papers (e.g., libnuma strategies).
- Previous internal notes: kv-cache-slab-buckets-and-eviction-draft.json (use case telemetry but not allocator design).

Unresolved near-term tasks

- Decide on large_object_threshold (Anne to propose based on telemetry).
- Confirm default slab sizes from 30-day production trace sample.
- Choose coalesce policy defaults for initial rollout (conservative recommended).

If you read this and have other micro-optimizations you've used in prior projects (e.g., range compaction heuristics, per-tenant weighted eviction), please drop notes inline or DM.
